title: In the beginning: six days and the Sabbath
summary:
God creates the heavens and the earth. Darkness is on the face of the deep; God speaks light, orders sky and sea and land, fills them with lights and living creatures, and makes humankind in his image, male and female. He sees that it is good. On the seventh day he rests and blesses that day.

As the opening of Genesis, the chapter sets what the rest of the book will work out.

The chapter matters inside that larger purpose: to tell how the world and Israel begin: creation, fracture, and God’s promise through Abraham’s line. A reader without prior theological training can still ask: what happens, who is named, what changes, and what should be understood.
purpose: Genesis 1 confesses one God as Maker. The world is not born from a war of gods. It is spoken, ordered, and given. The human being is not an accident: image and blessing come before any later fracture.
context:
Primeval history and the patriarchal age, remembered from Israel’s later life in the land. Traditional attribution to Moses; the book’s final shape is Israel’s origin story as received in the canon.

Narrative from creation to Joseph in Egypt. Names, genealogies, and family conflict carry the promise.

The book’s shape: Chs. 1–11 (beginnings of the world); 12–36 (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob); 37–50 (Joseph).
interpretations: Christians have long agreed that Genesis 1 confesses the one God as Maker of heaven and earth. They have not agreed on how the ‘days’ relate to later natural philosophy. Basil and Ambrose preach the days as ordered works of God without treating Genesis as a pagan theogony. Augustine, in the Literal Meaning of Genesis, warns against tying the faith to a single physical theory of the days. The disagreement is about the manner of the days, not about the Creator.
title_nl: In de begin: zes dagen en de Sabbat
summary_nl:
In de begin: zes dagen en de Sabbat. De namen die opkomen zijn God. Dit hoofdstuk van Genesis zet het verhaal voort onder die titel. Het is bedoeld om als gebeurtenis en spreken te volgen, niet als een motto los van de mensen die spreken.

Het opent in de buurt van de woorden: “In den beginne schiep God den hemel en de aarde..” Dat is een wegwijzer voor wat op het spel staat, geen vervanging van het hoofdstuk zelf. Het sluit naar: “En God zag al wat Hij gemaakt had, en ziet, het was zeer goed. Toen was het avond geweest, en het was morgen geweest, de zesde dag..” De beweging van opening naar slot is hoe het hoofdstuk leert.

Als opening van Genesis zet het hoofdstuk wat de rest van het boek zal uitwerken.

Het hoofdstuk telt binnen het grotere getuigenis van Genesis. Ook zonder vooropleiding kun je vragen: wat gebeurt er, wie wordt genoemd, wat verandert, en wat moet begrepen worden.
purpose_nl: Het doel van dit hoofdstuk is dat de lezer “In de begin: zes dagen en de Sabbat” verstaat als een nodige stap in Genesis, niet als los sieraad. Het opent Genesis en zet wat de volgende hoofdstukken uitwerken. Na het lezen is de vraag niet ‘welke weetjes heb ik verzameld?’ maar ‘wat moet ik nu verstaan dat ik eerder niet verstond?’

False prophets and prophetesses. The names that surface are Israel. The prophet’s word is aimed at a people, a city, or the nations. It judges, warns, and sometimes comforts.

It opens in the vicinity of the words: “And the word of the LORD came unto me, saying.” That is a signpost for what is at stake, not a replacement for the chapter itself. It closes toward: “Therefore ye shall see no more vanity, nor divine divinations: for I will deliver my people out of your hand: and ye shall know that I am th.” The movement from opening to close is how the chapter teaches.

In Ezekiel this is chapter 13 of 48, between what precedes and what follows. It is not an island.

The chapter matters inside that larger purpose: to show that the LORD is not bound to a fallen city, and that he can raise dry bones. A reader without prior theological training can still ask: what happens, who is named, what changes, and what should be understood.
purpose: The purpose of this chapter is that the reader understand “False prophets and prophetesses” as a necessary step in Ezekiel, not as a loose ornament. Vision, sign-act, and restoration. The prophet is ‘son of man’ before a holy God. It belongs between chapter 12 and chapter 14. After reading, the question is not ‘what trivia did I collect?’ but ‘what must I now understand that I did not understand before?’

title: The true vine
summary:
Jesus describes himself as the true vine and his Father as the gardener. The disciples are branches: they bear fruit only by remaining in him, and fruitless branches are taken away. He calls them friends rather than servants if they do what he commands, and he names the command: love one another as he has loved them. The chapter then turns: the world will hate them as it hated him first. The Spirit of truth will bear witness, and they also will bear witness.

The chapter moves from union and fruit (the vine) to the cost of that union (hatred and witness). Love is not a mood added at the end; it is the fruit of remaining.

The chapter matters because it names how life in Christ actually looks: not a private glow, but remaining, fruit, friendship, and a share in his rejection. A reader without prior study can still hear the image: a branch does not bear fruit by trying harder at a distance from the vine.
purpose: John 15 is the heart of the farewell: remaining in Christ, loving as he loves, and not being surprised by the world’s hatred. It looks back to chapter 14 (the way and the Spirit) and on to chapter 16 (the Spirit’s work and sorrow turned to joy). After reading, the disciple should understand that fruit, love, and persecution belong together in him.

title: Tobit’s piety in the Assyrian diaspora
summary:
Tobit, a Naphtalite in Nineveh after the Assyrian exile, keeps the law far from the land: he feeds the hungry, clothes the naked, and buries the dead at risk to himself. The chapter sets his piety and the cost of it in a foreign capital.

As the opening of Tobit, the chapter sets what the rest of the book will work out.

The chapter matters inside that larger purpose: to teach prayer, almsgiving, burial of the dead, marriage, and the hidden guidance of God. A reader without prior theological training can still ask: what happens, who is named, what changes, and what should be understood. Deuterocanonical status is not a reason to leave the chapter without a guide.
purpose: Tobit 1 shows Jewish faithfulness in the diaspora: alms, burial, and the law when the Temple is far. The later journey and healing hang on this character.
context: Second Temple Jews told this story of family piety under empire. The early Church kept Tobit among the books read for almsgiving and the burial of the dead. It is diaspora wisdom in narrative form, not a lesser Bible.
title_nl: Tobit’s piety in de Assyrian diaspora
summary_nl:
Tobit’s piety in de Assyrian diaspora. De namen die opkomen zijn Tobit. Dit hoofdstuk van Tobit zet het verhaal voort onder die titel. Het is bedoeld om als gebeurtenis en spreken te volgen, niet als een motto los van de mensen die spreken. Het hoofdstuk behoort tot de deuterocanon en krijgt hier dezelfde gids als de rest van de canon.

Het opent in de buurt van de woorden: “Het Boek der geschiedenissen van Tobias, de zoon van Tobias, de zoon van Ananiël, de zoon van Aduël, de zoon van Gabaël, uit het zaad van Azaël, uit de stam van.” Dat is een wegwijzer voor wat op het spel staat, geen vervanging van het hoofdstuk zelf. Achiachar nu was schenker, en zegelbewaarder, en huisverzorger, en rekenmees.” De beweging van opening naar slot is hoe het hoofdstuk leert.

Als opening van Tobit zet het hoofdstuk wat de rest van het boek zal uitwerken.

Het hoofdstuk telt binnen het grotere getuigenis van Tobit. Ook zonder vooropleiding kun je vragen: wat gebeurt er, wie wordt genoemd, wat verandert, en wat moet begrepen worden. Deuterocanoniek zijn is geen reden om het hoofdstuk zonder gids te laten.

context:
A Hellenistic Jewish voice, often associated with Alexandria, addressing kings in the language of both Israel and Greek philosophy. Usually placed in the late Second Temple / Hellenistic period. Traditional ascription to Solomon is a literary stance, not a modern author’s signature.

Exhortation to justice, the fate of the righteous, the nature of Wisdom, and a retelling of the exodus.

The book’s shape: Chs. 1–5 the just and the ungodly; 6–9 Wisdom; 10–19 Wisdom in Israel’s history, especially the exodus.

These books belong to the Greek Scriptures of Israel (the Septuagint) and to the Catholic and Orthodox canons. They are not a lesser Bible in this app: they receive the same chapter companion as the rest of the canon. Jews of the Second Temple period, and the early Church, read them. Protestant Bibles often print them separately or omit them. Wisdom literature of the diaspora: Greek diction, Jewish confession. The Fathers often heard the pre-existent Word in this book’s praise of Wisdom.

title: The mother and the seven sons
summary:
A mother and seven sons are tortured under Antiochus for refusing to eat swine’s flesh. They confess God as creator who will raise them; the king is told he will not escape judgment. The mother, last of all, dies after her children.

In 2 Maccabees this is chapter 7 of 15, between what precedes and what follows. It is not an island.

The chapter matters inside that larger purpose: to interpret the persecution as discipline and the martyrs as witnesses to resurrection. A reader without prior theological training can still ask: what happens, who is named, what changes, and what should be understood. Deuterocanonical status is not a reason to leave the chapter without a guide.
purpose: 2 Maccabees 7 is the book’s martyr-theology in a scene: resurrection of the body, creation from nothing, and faithfulness unto death. Historical narrative and confession are bound together; the chapter is not a parable pretending to be history, nor a bare casualty list.
context: The same Seleucid persecution as 1 Maccabees, told here as theological ‘pathetic history.’ Gregory of Nazianzus preached the brothers as martyrs; Augustine heard in them the hope of the resurrection of the body.

interpretations: 2 Maccabees 12 describes Judas making a sin-offering for fallen soldiers, with the narrator calling it a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead. The Latin Church, with Augustine, received prayer for the departed as consonant with this narrative. Many Protestant readers, not receiving the book as canonical, do not treat the passage as a rule of faith. The disagreement is real. The app reports the narrative and the history of its use; it does not pretend there was never a dispute.

It is meant to be followed as action and speech, not as a motto detached from the people who speak. As the close of 2 Maccabees, it should still have the previous chapter in the reader’s ear.

The chapter matters inside that larger purpose: to interpret the persecution as discipline and the martyrs as witnesses to resurrection. Deuterocanonical status is not a reason to leave the chapter without a guide.

context:
Jews in Ptolemaic Egypt, threatened in Alexandria’s hippodrome — not the Maccabean war in Judea. A Hellenistic Jewish work; the title ‘Maccabees’ is traditional, not a family chronicle.

Court danger, drunken elephants, prayer, reversal, and a feast of deliverance.

The book’s shape: Temple incident; the king’s rage; the hippodrome; deliverance and feast.

These books belong to the Greek Scriptures of Israel (the Septuagint) and to the Catholic and Orthodox canons. They are not a lesser Bible in this app: they receive the same chapter companion as the rest of the canon. Jews of the Second Temple period, and the early Church, read them. Protestant Bibles often print them separately or omit them. 3 Maccabees is in the Orthodox canon. It is Egyptian diaspora literature: persecution and Passover-like rescue in Alexandria.

title: Azariah’s prayer and the song of the three youths
summary:
In the furnace of Daniel 3, Azariah prays a confession for the people’s sins. An angel makes the fire as a dew. The three then sing a cosmic hymn: all works of the Lord, bless the Lord.

Prayer of Azariah is a single-chapter book in this Bible. What you meet at the start is the whole movement.

The chapter matters inside that larger purpose: to pray in the fire and to turn the furnace into a liturgy of creation. A reader without prior theological training can still ask: what happens, who is named, what changes, and what should be understood. Deuterocanonical status is not a reason to leave the chapter without a guide.
purpose: The addition turns the furnace into liturgy: repentance, rescue, and the praise of creation. The Church sings the Song of the Three as the Benedicite.
context:
The furnace of Daniel 3, expanded in Greek with a confession and the Song of the Three. A Greek addition within Daniel 3.

Penitential prayer, then a cosmic hymn: all works of the Lord, bless the Lord.

The book’s shape: Azariah’s prayer; the angel; the song of the three youths.

These books belong to the Greek Scriptures of Israel (the Septuagint) and to the Catholic and Orthodox canons. They are not a lesser Bible in this app: they receive the same chapter companion as the rest of the canon. Jews of the Second Temple period, and the early Church, read them. Protestant Bibles often print them separately or omit them. The Church sings the Song of the Three in festal worship. It is not a separate novel: it is Daniel 3 opened into praise.
title_nl: Azariah’s prayer en de lied van de three youths
summary_nl:
Azariah’s prayer en de lied van de three youths. De namen die opkomen zijn Azariah. Het hoofdstuk is gebed en lied. Iemand spreekt tot God, of wordt aangesproken, met lof, droefheid, vertrouwen of hoop — geen koningskroniek. Het hoofdstuk behoort tot de deuterocanon en krijgt hier dezelfde gids als de rest van de canon.

Het opent in de buurt van de woorden: “En zij wandelden in het midden der vlam, zingende God, en lovende de Here..” Dat is een wegwijzer voor wat op het spel staat, geen vervanging van het hoofdstuk zelf. Het sluit naar: “Gij allen die de Here vreest looft de God der goden, prijst hem en dankt hem, want zijn barmhartigheid duurt in alle eeuwigheid..” De beweging van opening naar slot is hoe het hoofdstuk leert.

Gebed van Azarja is in deze Bijbel een boek van één hoofdstuk. Wat je aan het begin ontmoet, is de hele beweging.

Het hoofdstuk telt binnen het grotere getuigenis van Gebed van Azarja. Ook zonder vooropleiding kun je vragen: wat gebeurt er, wie wordt genoemd, wat verandert, en wat moet begrepen worden. Deuterocanoniek zijn is geen reden om het hoofdstuk zonder gids te laten.
purpose_nl: Het doel van dit hoofdstuk is dat de lezer “Azariah’s prayer en de lied van de three youths” verstaat als een nodige stap in Gebed van Azarja, niet als los sieraad. Na het lezen is de vraag niet ‘welke weetjes heb ik verzameld?’ maar ‘wat moet ik nu verstaan dat ik eerder niet verstond?’
context_nl:
Gebed van Azarja staat in de canon als gebed en lied. Lees dit eerste hoofdstuk als ingang tot het geheel, niet als losse spreuk.

Het boek behoort tot de deuterocanon: dezelfde Kerk leest het, met dezelfde eerbied voor de Schrift zelf.
